notes.front: What is Azure Virtual Machines?
notes.back: An Azure service that gives you virtualised servers without buying or maintaining the physical hardware that runs them.
notes.explanation: You keep the flexibility of virtualisation, while the hardware underneath is not yours to buy or maintain.
notes.example: Like renting a fully furnished flat instead of buying a house: you live in it and look after it, but someone else owns the building.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Virtual machines in Azure”
notes.evidence: An Azure virtual machine gives you the flexibility of virtualization without having to buy and maintain the physical hardware that runs it.

notes.front: In Azure, what is a virtual machine image?
notes.back: A ready-made template holding an operating system, and possibly tools, from which you can deploy a virtual machine quickly.
notes.explanation: Prebuilt images are what let you deploy virtual machines quickly.
notes.example: Like a cake mix with the dry ingredients already measured: you add a little and bake, rather than starting from flour.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Describe Azure virtual machines”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets?
notes.back: A way to create and manage a group of load-balanced virtual machines whose number can grow or shrink automatically.
notes.explanation: The count can change in response to demand or to a schedule you define.
notes.example: Like a supermarket that opens more tills when the queues grow and closes them when the shop is quiet.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?, “What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?”
notes.evidence: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of load balanced virtual machines (VM) instances. The number of VM instances can automatically increase or decrease in response to demand or a defined schedule.

notes.front: What is an availability set?
notes.back: A logical grouping of virtual machines that lowers the chance of one correlated failure taking related machines down together.
notes.explanation: It spreads the machines across several fault domains, which the docs call especially useful in regions without availability zones.
notes.example: Like a hospital running its backup generators from separate fuse boards, so one blown fuse cannot cut them all.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “What is an availability set?”
notes.evidence: Availability sets are logical groupings of VMs that reduce the chance of correlated failures bringing down related VMs at the same time. Availability sets distribute VMs across multiple fault domains, improving reliability. This configuration is especially useful in regions that don't support availability zones.

notes.front: In an availability set, what is an update domain?
notes.back: A group of virtual machines, and the physical hardware under them, that can be restarted at the same time.
notes.explanation: The group includes the hardware under the machines, so machines and hardware restart together.
notes.example: Like a school that sends one year group home at a time while the heating is repaired, so lessons never stop entirely.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “Update domains”
notes.evidence: Update domains indicate groups of virtual machines and underlying physical hardware that can be restarted at the same time.

notes.front: In an availability set, what is a fault domain?
notes.back: A group of virtual machines that share a common power source and network switch.
notes.explanation: By default, an availability set separates its machines across up to three fault domains.
notes.example: Like houses on one street that share a substation: when it trips, all of them lose power together.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “Fault domains”
notes.evidence: Fault domains define the group of virtual machines that share a common power source and network switch. By default, the virtual machines configured within your availability set are separated across up to three fault domains.

notes.front: What is Azure Virtual Desktop?
notes.back: A service running on Azure that virtualises Windows desktops and apps so users can reach them remotely.
notes.explanation: The desktops and apps stay in the cloud, and users connect to them from their own devices.
notes.example: Like streaming a film instead of owning the disc: the content lives elsewhere and you watch it from whatever screen you have.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Virtual Desktop?, “What is Azure Virtual Desktop?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure, what is a container?
notes.back: A lightweight virtualisation environment; many can run on one physical or virtual host, and you do not manage an operating system for each.
notes.explanation: Containers are built to be created, scaled out and stopped quickly as demand changes.
notes.example: Like shipping crates on one cargo ship: each keeps its own goods separate, but they all share the same hull and engine.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “What are containers?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Container Instances (ACI)?
notes.back: The fastest and simplest way to run Linux or Windows containers in Azure, with no virtual machines or higher-level service to manage.
notes.explanation: It runs both Linux and Windows containers.
notes.example: Like hailing a taxi for one trip: no car to own, no fleet to run, just the journey you need.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Container Instances?, “What is Azure Container Instances?”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Instances offers the fastest and simplest way to run Linux or Windows containers in Azure, without having to manage any virtual machines and without having to adopt a higher-level service.

notes.front: What is Azure Container Apps?
notes.back: A serverless platform for running containerised applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Container Apps takes on configuring servers, orchestrating containers and deployment details for you.
notes.example: Like a ride-hailing service that sends more cars as bookings rise, rather than a single taxi you hail yourself.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Container Apps overview, “Azure Container Apps overview”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Apps is a serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing the underlying infrastructure. Instead of configuring servers, orchestrating containers, and handling deployment details yourself, let Container Apps provide the up-to-date resources that keep your applications stable, secure, and scalable.

notes.front: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?
notes.back: A managed Kubernetes service for deploying and managing containerised applications.
notes.explanation: It moves much of the complexity and operational overhead of running Kubernetes onto Azure.
notes.example: Like hiring a harbour master to schedule a whole port of ships, rather than steering each boat yourself.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?, “What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?”
notes.evidence: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes service for deploying and managing containerized applications. AKS offloads the complexity and operational overhead of managing Kubernetes to Azure.

notes.front: What is a microservice architecture?
notes.back: A design that breaks a solution into smaller, independent parts, often each in its own container.
notes.explanation: Each part can then be maintained, scaled or updated on its own.
notes.example: Like a restaurant kitchen split into stations for starters, mains and desserts, each staffed and stocked on its own.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “Use containers in your solutions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Functions?
notes.back: A serverless service for building apps with less code, less infrastructure and lower costs.
notes.explanation: Instead of deploying and maintaining servers, you rely on the cloud to supply the resources the app needs.
notes.example: Like a motion-sensor light: it switches on only when someone walks past, and costs nothing while the hall is empty.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Functions?, “What is Azure Functions?”
notes.evidence: Azure Functions is a serverless solution that allows you to build robust apps while using less code, and with less infrastructure and lower costs. Instead of worrying about deploying and maintaining servers, you can use the cloud infrastructure to provide all the up-to-date resources needed to keep your applications running.

notes.front: What are Durable Functions?
notes.back: Azure Functions that keep state: the runtime passes a context through the function to track what happened before.
notes.explanation: Ordinary functions are stateless by default and act as if they start afresh on every event.
notes.example: Like a relay baton carrying a note of each runner's split time, so the next runner knows the race so far.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure App Service?
notes.back: A platform for running web applications, mobile back ends and RESTful APIs without managing the underlying infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Microsoft describes it as a web hosting service that handles the heavy lifting so you can focus on the app.
notes.example: Like renting a stall in a managed market hall: you run your shop, the landlord handles the roof, lights and security.
notes.source: Azure documentation: App Service overview, “App Service overview”
notes.evidence: Azure App Service is a platform that lets you run web applications, mobile back ends, and RESTful APIs without worrying about managing the underlying infrastructure. Think of it as a powerful web hosting service that takes care of all the heavy lifting for you, so you can focus on creating great applications.

notes.front: In Azure App Service, what are WebJobs?
notes.back: A feature that runs a program or script in the same context as a web, mobile or back-end app, on a schedule or a trigger.
notes.explanation: They are often used for background tasks that belong to the application's logic.
notes.example: Like a shop's night cleaner who works in the same premises after hours, rather than in a separate building.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe application hosting options, “WebJobs”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an App Service plan?
notes.back: The set of compute resources that an App Service web app runs on.
notes.explanation: An App Service app always runs in one.
notes.example: Like a shared office floor you lease: every team you put on it uses the same desks and power.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure App Service plans?, “What are Azure App Service plans?”
notes.evidence: An *Azure App Service plan* defines a set of compute resources for a web app to run. An app service always runs in an App Service plan.

notes.front: Once you create an Azure virtual machine, who configures and patches the software on it?
notes.back: You do: configuring, patching and installing its software stay your tasks.
notes.explanation: Azure removes the physical hardware, but the machine itself is still yours to maintain.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Virtual machines in Azure”
notes.evidence: However, you still need to maintain the virtual machine by performing tasks, such as configuring, patching, and installing the software that runs on it.

notes.front: Azure Virtual Machines run virtualised servers as {{c1::infrastructure as a service}}.
notes.back: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS).
notes.explanation: As with a physical server, you control the operating system and the software installed on it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Describe Azure virtual machines”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of Azure virtual machines gives a quick way to build a computer with the exact configuration needed to code and test an application?
notes.back: Development and test.
notes.explanation: Azure lets you create a machine with exactly the configuration the application needs.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Virtual machines in Azure”
notes.evidence: Development and test – Azure virtual machines offer a quick and easy way to create a computer with specific configurations required to code and test an application.

notes.front: Which use of Azure virtual machines connects machines in Azure to your organisation's own network?
notes.back: Extending your datacentre.
notes.explanation: The machines sit in an Azure network that can easily be connected to the organisation's network.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Virtual machines in Azure”
notes.evidence: virtual machines in an Azure virtual network can easily be connected to your organization’s network.

notes.front: When you provision an Azure virtual machine, which choice sets its purpose, number of processor cores and amount of memory?
notes.back: Its size.
notes.explanation: Size is one of three resource choices, alongside storage disks and networking.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “VM resources and sizing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When you provision an Azure virtual machine, which resource choice covers hard disk drives versus solid-state drives?
notes.back: Its storage disks.
notes.explanation: Disk configuration affects storage capacity and throughput.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “VM resources and sizing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When you provision an Azure virtual machine, which resource choice covers its network, public address and port settings?
notes.back: Its networking.
notes.explanation: Networking completes the trio of choices with size and storage disks.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “VM resources and sizing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the size you choose for an Azure virtual machine determine?
notes.back: Factors such as processing power, memory, storage capacity and network bandwidth.
notes.explanation: You pick the size from the workload you want to run.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Sizes and pricing”
notes.evidence: The size of the virtual machine that you use is determined by the workload that you want to run. The size that you choose then determines factors such as processing power, memory, storage capacity, and network bandwidth.

notes.front: How does Azure charge for a running virtual machine, and how is its storage billed?
notes.back: An hourly price based on size and operating system, charging only used minutes for partial hours; storage is charged separately.
notes.explanation: You pay for the minutes a machine runs rather than for whole hours.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Virtual machines in Azure, “Sizes and pricing”
notes.evidence: Azure charges an hourly price based on the virtual machine’s size and operating system. For partial hours, Azure charges only for the minutes used. Storage is priced and charged separately.

notes.front: Which type of Azure virtual machine size offers a balanced ratio of processor to memory?
notes.back: General purpose.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest it for testing and development, small to medium databases and low to medium traffic web servers.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure, “General purpose”
notes.evidence: General purpose VM sizes provide balanced CPU-to-memory ratio. Ideal for testing and development, small to medium databases, and low to medium traffic web servers.

notes.front: Which Azure virtual machine family is burstable and cost-efficient, suiting test machines with occasional processor spikes?
notes.back: The B-series.
notes.explanation: The training contrasts it with the general-purpose D-series used for web and app servers.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Understand VM size families and names”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Azure virtual machine family is memory optimised, for in-memory databases and analytics?
notes.back: The E-series.
notes.explanation: For an even larger memory footprint, such as large enterprise databases, the training points to the M-series.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Understand VM size families and names”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does an Azure virtual machine size name encode?
notes.back: Characters for the family, the number of virtual processors and extra features such as premium storage or accelerators.
notes.explanation: Each character stands for a different aspect of the machine.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure, “VM size and series naming”
notes.evidence: Each character in the name represents different aspects of the VM. These include the VM family, number of vCPUs, and extra features like premium storage or included accelerators.

notes.front: What can make the number of virtual machines in a scale set change automatically?
notes.back: Demand, or a schedule you define.
notes.explanation: Instances are added as demand rises and removed as it falls, or follow a schedule you set.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?, “What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?”
notes.evidence: The number of VM instances can automatically increase or decrease in response to demand or a defined schedule.

notes.front: Is there a charge for the scale set itself when you use Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets?
notes.back: No; you pay only for the compute, network and storage resources the scale set uses.
notes.explanation: The charge comes only from the compute, network and storage the instances consume.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?, “Why use Virtual Machine Scale Sets?”
notes.evidence: There's no extra cost for using scale sets. You're charged based on the compute, network, and storage resources that the scale set uses.

notes.front: Does a scale set on its own protect you against the failure of a datacentre?
notes.back: No; you need to spread its machines across availability zones for that.
notes.explanation: Deploying the instances across zones is what protects against a datacentre failing.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?, “Why use Virtual Machine Scale Sets?”
notes.evidence: A scale set alone can't protect you against data center failures. Deploying VMs across Availability Zones within a scale set can protect you against data center failure.

notes.front: What must you deploy in an availability set to meet its 99.95% service-level agreement?
notes.back: Two or more virtual machines.
notes.explanation: Two or more machines in the set keep the application highly available.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “What is an availability set?”
notes.evidence: Using two or more VMs in an availability set helps keep applications highly available and meets the 99.95% Azure service-level agreement (SLA).

notes.front: What do you pay for when you use an availability set?
notes.back: Only the virtual machines in it; the availability set costs nothing extra.
notes.explanation: Like a scale set, an availability set is a grouping over machines you already pay for.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “What is an availability set?”
notes.evidence: There's no extra cost for using availability sets. You only pay for each VM instance that you create.

notes.front: What are the most fault domains and update domains an availability set can have?
notes.back: Up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains.
notes.explanation: These settings are fixed once the availability set has been created.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “How do availability sets work?”
notes.evidence: Each availability set can have up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains. These settings can't be changed after the availability set is created.

notes.front: During planned maintenance, how many update domains in an availability set are restarted at once?
notes.back: One at a time, though not necessarily in order.
notes.explanation: A restarted update domain gets 30 minutes to recover before work starts on another.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “Update domains”
notes.evidence: The order of update domains being restarted might not proceed sequentially during planned maintenance, but only one update domain is restarted at a time. A restarted update domain has 30 minutes to recover before maintenance starts on a different update domain.

notes.front: Does placing virtual machines in an availability set protect an application from operating system or application failures?
notes.back: No; it only limits the impact of physical hardware failures, network outages and power interruptions.
notes.explanation: Availability sets separate hardware, not software.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “Fault domains”
notes.evidence: Placing your virtual machines into an availability set doesn't protect your application from operating system or application-specific failures. But it does limit the impact of potential physical hardware failures, network outages, or power interruptions.

notes.front: In regions that support availability zones, which design does the Microsoft training say is often preferred over availability sets?
notes.back: Zone-based designs, which are often preferred for their broader failure isolation.
notes.explanation: The training keeps availability sets for machine-level redundancy within a region.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Virtual machine availability sets”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Virtual Desktop, what is the difference between single-session and multi-session?
notes.back: Single-session gives each device to one user; multi-session shares machines among users for scalability.
notes.explanation: Both deliver a full Windows experience with Windows 11, Windows 10 or Windows Server.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Virtual Desktop?, “What is Azure Virtual Desktop?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With Azure Virtual Desktop, which parts do you still manage yourself?
notes.back: Only the image and virtual machines used for sessions; Azure runs supporting roles such as the gateway and broker.
notes.explanation: That differs from traditional Remote Desktop Services, where you run those roles yourself.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Virtual Desktop?, “Key capabilities”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How fast can Azure Container Instances start containers?
notes.back: In seconds, without provisioning or managing virtual machines.
notes.explanation: There are no virtual machines for you to provision or manage first.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Container Instances?, “Fast startup times”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Instances can start containers in Azure in seconds, without the need to provision and manage VMs.

notes.front: How is Azure Container Instances billed?
notes.back: By the second, for the exact processor cores and memory you specify.
notes.explanation: Exact sizing lets you tune spending to what the container actually needs.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Container Instances?, “Custom sizes”
notes.evidence: You pay based on what you need and get billed by the second, so you can fine-tune your spending based on actual need.

notes.front: Azure Container Instances is a {{c1::platform as a service}} offering: you upload containers and it runs them.
notes.back: Platform as a service (PaaS).
notes.explanation: You manage neither virtual machines nor extra services to run the container.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “Azure Container Instances”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On what can Azure Container Apps scale an application?
notes.back: Web request traffic, event-driven processing, and processor or memory load, among other scalers.
notes.explanation: The list is open: other supported scalers can be used too.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Container Apps overview, “Azure Container Apps overview”
notes.evidence: applications built on Azure Container Apps can dynamically scale based on the following characteristics: - HTTP traffic - Event-driven processing - CPU or memory load - Any KEDA-supported scaler

notes.front: What are two common uses of Azure Container Apps?
notes.back: Any two of: endpoints for web APIs, background processing jobs, event-driven processing, microservices.
notes.explanation: The docs list these four as common uses.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Container Apps overview, “Azure Container Apps overview”
notes.evidence: Common uses of Azure Container Apps include: - Deploying API endpoints - Hosting background processing jobs - Handling event-driven processing - Running microservices

notes.front: In Azure Kubernetes Service, what do you pay for?
notes.back: Only the nodes that run your applications.
notes.explanation: Azure takes care of critical operations such as health monitoring and maintenance.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?, “Overview of AKS”
notes.evidence: Azure takes care of critical operations like health monitoring and maintenance, and you only pay for the AKS nodes that run your applications.

notes.front: What are the two cluster modes of Azure Kubernetes Service, and which is recommended for most teams?
notes.back: AKS Automatic and AKS Standard; Automatic is recommended for most teams and workloads.
notes.explanation: In Automatic, Azure handles node management, scaling, security, monitoring and upgrades.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?, “What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?”
notes.evidence: AKS offers two cluster modes: - **AKS Automatic**: A fully managed experience with production-ready defaults. Azure handles node management, scaling, security, monitoring, and upgrades automatically. Recommended for most teams and workloads. - **AKS Standard**: Full control over cluster configuration and node pool management.

notes.front: In a microservice architecture, what can you do when only the back end reaches capacity?
notes.back: Scale the back end on its own, leaving the front end and storage as they are.
notes.explanation: Each part runs independently, so each can be scaled or changed separately.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “Use containers in your solutions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With Azure Functions, what starts your code running?
notes.back: An event wakes the function, so no resources need to stay provisioned when there are no events.
notes.explanation: Apps on virtual machines or containers need those resources running for the app to work.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Describe Azure functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kinds of trigger commonly run an Azure function?
notes.back: An event (often a web request), a timer, or a message from another Azure service.
notes.explanation: Functions suit work that can be finished quickly, within seconds or less.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Microsoft training, what does Azure charge for when a function runs?
notes.back: Only the processor time used while the function runs.
notes.explanation: Resources are released automatically when the function finishes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are Azure functions stateless or stateful by default?
notes.back: Stateless: each behaves as if it restarts every time it responds to an event.
notes.explanation: Keeping state needs Durable Functions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Azure Functions hosting plan is recommended, offering fast event-driven scaling and pay-as-you-go billing?
notes.back: The Flex Consumption plan.

notes.source: Azure documentation: What is Azure Functions?, “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: Flex Consumption plan | **Recommended.** Fast event-driven scaling, virtual network integration, and pay-as-you-go billing.

notes.front: Which operating systems can Azure App Service run apps on, and what can you deploy if your app is containerised?
notes.back: Windows and Linux; a containerised app can be deployed as a custom container.
notes.explanation: App Service runs several web stacks, including Java, Node.js and Python, on either system.
notes.source: Azure documentation: App Service overview, “App Service overview”
notes.evidence: Node.js, Python, and PHP, and can run them on both Windows and Linux. Or, if your app is containerized, you can just deploy it as a custom container.

notes.front: Which App Service app type gives full support for hosting websites in languages such as Java, Ruby, Node.js or Python?
notes.back: Web apps.
notes.explanation: You choose Windows or Linux as the host operating system.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe application hosting options, “Web apps”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which App Service app type builds back ends for iOS and Android apps, with push notifications and social sign-in?
notes.back: Mobile apps.

notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe application hosting options, “Mobile apps”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When WebJobs run, whose compute do they use?
notes.back: The processor and memory of the App Service plan's virtual machine instances, like the apps.

notes.evidence: If you enable diagnostic logs, perform backups, or run WebJobs, they also use CPU cycles and memory on these VM instances.

notes.front: What are two things an App Service plan defines?
notes.back: Any two of: operating system, region, number of instances, instance size, pricing tier.

notes.evidence: Each App Service plan defines: - Operating system (Windows, Linux) - Region (West US, East US, and so on) - Number of virtual machine (VM) instances - Size of VM instances (small, medium, large) - Pricing tier

notes.front: When several apps share one App Service plan, what happens when you scale the plan?
notes.back: All the apps scale together.
notes.explanation: They share the same underlying compute instances.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure App Service plans?, “Considerations for running and scaling an app”
notes.evidence: All apps in an App Service plan scale together, because they share the same underlying compute resources (VM instances).

notes.front: In the Free and Shared App Service tiers, whose apps share the virtual machine your app runs on?
notes.back: Other App Service apps, including apps of other customers.
notes.explanation: These two base tiers allocate processor quotas to each app.

notes.evidence: Free and Shared, the two base tiers, run an app on the same Azure VM as other App Service apps, including apps of other customers. These tiers allocate CPU quotas to each app that you run.

notes.front: A team must install custom software and tune the operating system of a legacy accounting server. Which Azure compute option fits?
notes.back: Azure Virtual Machines.

notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Describe Azure virtual machines”

notes.front: A start-up wants to host a web shop and its web APIs without managing servers, with automatic scaling. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure App Service.
notes.explanation: App Service hosts web apps and APIs with automatic scaling and high availability, and no infrastructure to manage.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe application hosting options, “Azure App Service”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A photo site needs a thumbnail made whenever an image is uploaded, and uploads are rare and bursty. Which option fits best?
notes.back: Azure Functions.
notes.explanation: Functions run short pieces of code when an event occurs and scale with demand, with nothing kept running between events.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Describe Azure functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester needs to run one containerised tool for an afternoon without setting up virtual machines or an orchestrator. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure Container Instances.
notes.explanation: It is the fastest and simplest way to run a container, with no machines or higher-level service to manage.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “Azure Container Instances”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants serverless containers for several microservices, with built-in load balancing and scaling. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure Container Apps.

notes.back: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).
notes.explanation: Orchestration manages container lifecycles and simplifies running a fleet.

notes.front: A call centre wants contractors on personal laptops to use identical Windows desktops, with no company data stored on the laptops. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure Virtual Desktop.
notes.explanation: It delivers centrally managed cloud desktops, keeping apps and data in Azure-hosted sessions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual desktop, “When to use Azure Virtual Desktop”

notes.front: An online ticket seller's traffic triples every evening. It wants identical virtual machines added and removed automatically. What should it use?
notes.back: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets.
notes.explanation: Scale sets keep instances identical and scale out or in with demand or a schedule.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Virtual machine scale sets”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm must run two virtual machines in a region with no availability zones and wants to limit the damage from one power or network failure. What should it use?
notes.back: An availability set.
notes.explanation: Availability sets spread machines across fault domains and are especially useful where zones are unavailable.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “What is an availability set?”
notes.evidence: Availability sets distribute VMs across multiple fault domains, improving reliability. This configuration is especially useful in regions that don't support availability zones.

notes.front: An availability set has five update domains and holds seven virtual machines. Which update domain does the sixth machine join?
notes.back: The first update domain, the same as the first machine.
notes.explanation: Placement wraps round: the seventh machine joins the second update domain.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “Update domains”
notes.evidence: If more than five VMs are configured in an availability set with five update domains, the sixth VM is placed in the same update domain as the first, the seventh with the second, and so on.

notes.front: Planned host maintenance and a failed network switch each threaten your virtual machines. Which kind of domain guards against each?
notes.back: Update domains guard against planned maintenance; fault domains guard against shared power or network failures.
notes.explanation: The training groups machines both ways inside an availability set.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Virtual machine availability sets”

notes.front: Which of these is the customer's job on an Azure virtual machine: replacing a failed disk in the rack, or patching the guest operating system?
notes.back: Patching the guest operating system.
notes.explanation: Azure removes the need to buy and maintain server hardware, but patching inside the machine stays with you.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure virtual machines, “Describe Azure virtual machines”

notes.front: A web app on App Service needs a script that tidies old uploads every night, running in the same context as the app. Which App Service feature fits?
notes.back: WebJobs.
notes.explanation: WebJobs run a program or script alongside an App Service app, on a schedule or a trigger.

notes.front: An analytics virtual machine keeps running out of memory. Which of its resource choices do you change: size, storage disks or networking?
notes.back: Its size.
notes.explanation: Size sets the machine's processor cores and memory; disks and networking cover storage and connectivity.

notes.front: What is the key difference between a virtual machine and a container in who manages the operating system?
notes.back: Each virtual machine runs its own operating system you manage; for a container you do not manage the operating system.
notes.explanation: Virtual machines are limited to one operating system each, whereas many containers can share a host.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “What are containers?”

notes.front: How do Azure Functions differ from virtual machines and containers in what must be running?
notes.back: Virtual machines and containers must stay running for the app to work; a function is woken by an event.
notes.explanation: That is why functions need no resources provisioned while no events arrive.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Describe Azure functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do Azure Container Apps add over Azure Container Instances?
notes.back: Built-in load balancing and scaling.
notes.explanation: Both are platform-as-a-service ways to run containers without managing them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure containers, “Azure Container Apps”

notes.front: How do availability sets compare with availability zones for resiliency and latency?
notes.back: Sets: lower latency, as machines sit closer, but exposed to datacentre-level failures. Zones: more resilient, spreading machines across separate datacentres.
notes.explanation: A datacentre-level network outage can affect several fault domains in a set at once.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Availability sets overview, “What is an availability set?”
notes.evidence: Availability sets provide lower VM-to-VM latency than availability zones because the VMs are placed in closer physical proximity. Availability sets have fault isolation for many possible failures, to minimize single points of failure and to offer high availability. Availability sets are still susceptible to certain shared infrastructure failures, such as datacenter-level network outages, which can affect multiple fault domains.

notes.front: When hosting a web app, how does a virtual machine differ from Azure App Service?
notes.back: A virtual machine gives maximum control of the hosting environment; App Service runs the app without you managing infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Virtual machines may also be the most familiar option for newcomers to the cloud.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe application hosting options, “Describe application hosting options”
